questions.question: Do you use a gas burner purely out of necessity? I know you also use the wok on your induction.

hybrid.answer:
No, it's not just necessity. I prefer a portable gas burner for wok cooking because it works better. A butane burner rated at 12,500 BTU or more works better than a standard home burner, even one with a higher BTU rating [1]. Even when I had a full gas range at home, a small portable butane burner worked better for wok cooking [2].

**Why the portable burner wins:** Portable burners have a very concentrated flame pointing at the center. A home range spreads its heat out evenly, so with a wok a lot of that energy flows up the sides and heats the air instead of the metal [3].

**Induction:** My new wok works on induction. You can get good stir-frying out of it, but not wok flavor [4]. I can cook the vast majority of dishes on induction without trouble [5]. A gas flame is essential for dishes that rely on wok hei, like fried rice or dry-fried beef chow fun [6]. On induction, the workaround is a blowtorch, which gets you some of the smokiness but doesn't taste quite the same [7].

questions.question: How often do you oil your wooden cutting boards and utensils?

hybrid.answer:
I oil them as needed rather than on a schedule. For the cutting board that's probably a few times a year, and my wooden utensils get oiled less often than they should [1][2].

**How I know it's time:** A freshly oiled board gets a hydrophobic coating where water beads up. As that wears off, water starts soaking in. When I see big stains developing, or the board gets hard to clean, I re-oil it [2].

**How I do it:** I use Howard Butcher Block Conditioner and rub it in with a paper towel or an oil rag [2][3].

**When it's really beat up:** If the board gets badly worn or stained, I sand it with an orbital sander. At one point I also trimmed the sides with a table saw, sanded everything and rounded the corners again to make it nearly new [3].

questions.question: Would you recommend a cleaver for breaking down the turkey frame? Any specific one?

hybrid.answer:
Yes, I'd recommend a cleaver for breaking down the turkey frame, and the one I'd point you to is a Shibazi Chinese cleaver [1]. It's a Chinese-style cleaver that you can get online for about 40 or 50 bucks, as best I remember [2]. I use it a lot because it stays sharp, the metal is pretty hard, and it's nice and heavy, so it gets through a turkey carcass easily [2]. They come in an 8 and a 9 inch size, and I think mine is the 9 [2].

A cleaver also helps with spatchcocking. If your kitchen shears can't get through a tough bone, use the cleaver to work through whatever is giving you resistance [3]. For the shears themselves, I use OXO [4].

questions.question: When should I salt my steak?

hybrid.answer:
I salt my steak well ahead of cooking: at least 45 minutes before, and ideally overnight, left uncovered in the fridge [1][2].

**Why ahead of time:**
- The salt first pulls moisture out, then the brine breaks down some muscle proteins and the steak reabsorbs that moisture. Because those proteins are broken down, they tighten up less when cooked, so less moisture gets squeezed out. You get a juicier steak with better seasoning throughout [3].
- Leaving it uncovered dries the surface, which makes it less hospitable to bacteria, builds a pellicle, and makes the steak sear better [4].
- In a side-by-side with tenderloin, the salted-and-rested steak got a much deeper mahogany crust and held its juices better than the unsalted one [5][6].

**If you're short on time:** 45 minutes is about the minimum for this to happen, and it's what I do for a quick version [3]. You can also just sear straight away, but don't cook it once a lot of moisture has beaded on the surface, because that moisture sucks heat from the pan [7].

**Don't go too far:** I once salted a steak for 4 days and it ended up with a texture almost like ham [8]. Ultimately, how you like the texture is a matter of personal preference, and an unsalted steak can still be great [6][9].

questions.question: Is the reverse sear still the best way to cook a steak?

hybrid.answer:
Yes. The reverse sear is still my favorite way to cook a big steak, nearly 20 years after I wrote about it for Cook's Illustrated [1]. For a thick steak like a big ribeye, it's the way to go [2].

- **Why I like it:** You get a much more even cook from edge to center, instead of the bullseye pattern you get with the traditional sear-then-oven method [3].
- **Wider margin for error:** The window of perfect doneness is much wider, probably 10 to 20 minutes before it starts to overcook in the oven, compared with a very small window when cooking hot and fast [4].
- **Versus sous vide:** I actually prefer it to sous vide, because the dry surface lets you sear better and render the fat better [5].
- **No rest needed:** Because you only sear briefly at the end, the temperature is already normalized, so you can cut right in [6].

**Caveat:** It works best on thick steaks. It's not really worth it for anything thinner than about an inch and a half [7]. The traditional sear-then-oven method works fine too, and it's the better choice if your goal is to cook steaks fast [3][8].

questions.question: Which non-stick pan should I buy?

hybrid.answer:
I'd buy the Titanium Pro, the non-coated pan I co-designed with Our Place. I partnered with the company on it, so weigh that when you consider my pick [1]. It's the pan I use for virtually all of my non-wok cooking these days [2]. It sears nicely and evenly, it sears faster, and I can use metal utensils in it [3].

**The trade-off:** It's not as non-stick as Teflon, but I think it's better in most other respects [4].

**Teflon-style coated pans:** I wouldn't use one for searing [5]. The coating has a very limited lifespan [6]. If you only want one for a specific job, I still use non-stick for something like an omelet [7].

**Cast iron:** I'd pick it if I wanted the best possible sear and was willing to put in a bit more time and work [8].

questions.question: Is jarred pre-chopped garlic any good?

hybrid.answer:
No, I'd stay away from jarred pre-chopped garlic, especially the kind packed in water or olive oil, because there's hardly any garlic flavor left in it [1]. Fresh garlic that you peel yourself is the best [2].

- **Why it's different:** Once garlic is cut, its flavor starts to change and you can't change it back, so any pre-minced or pre-cut garlic tastes different from natural garlic [3].
- **Citric acid versions:** Two of the samples had a strong citric acid flavor. Citric acid is a preservative that controls water activity and texture, but it also completely changes the flavor. I wouldn't recommend those, certainly not raw [4].
- **Cooking:** If you're going to cook with them, they can work, since cooking tames the sharper pungent flavors and evens out some of the difference [4][5]. Even so, there's not much aroma to them [5].
- **Better shortcuts:** Pre-peeled cloves are fine for most things, especially if you're cooking them, and garlic paste may be an acceptable substitute [2][1]. Pre-minced garlic is the one I'd stay away from [6].

questions.question: Do you ever inject your turkey? And if so, any recommendations on what to use?

hybrid.answer:
I rarely inject my turkey. I've done it in the past, but it's not something I typically do [1]. When you inject, whatever you put in doesn't get inside the muscle fibers; it sloshes around and separates some of them. The turkey comes out moist the way a sponge is wet, rather than the way a juicy piece of meat is [1].

That said, I've enjoyed injected turkeys, and if you do inject, here's what I'd use:

- **Well-seasoned stock:** Something with salt in it essentially brines the turkey from the inside as well as the outside, which helps it retain more moisture when you cook and slice it [2].
- **Stock and brown butter:** I've done injections with a mixture of turkey stock and brown butter, and I think it can be delicious [2][3].
- **Herb-infused stock or herb butter:** You can simmer turkey stock with a lot of herbs, or melt an herb butter, combine it with the stock and inject that [3].

questions.question: Why do you wash meat before stir-frying?

hybrid.answer:
I wash sliced beef because it makes the texture noticeably better. In side-by-side tests while working on my book, it made a huge difference [1].

- **Room for marinade:** Squeezing and massaging the meat in plenty of cold water pushes out some of the excess juices. That leaves more room for the marinade to penetrate, so you get more flavor in the meat [1].
- **More tender texture:** Washing also loosens up the texture of the muscle, so the beef comes out more tender, and the difference is stark when you compare side by side [1].
- **Hard water:** A friend of mine had the idea that in places with hard water, the slightly alkaline makeup of the water may also affect the beef. That was his idea, not something I've established [1].

After washing, I squeeze the meat out in a fine mesh strainer so the excess water doesn't water down the marinade [2]. I never used to wash meat until I started testing it [3]. I also say the washing step would improve the beef in my older beef and broccoli video, which doesn't include it [4].

questions.question: Just wondering, what is the best way to clean the wok after each use? And should I use the heat & coat in oil technique after each use as well?

hybrid.answer:
My routine after each use: rinse the wok out (soap is fine if you need it), put it on a burner, heat it until it's completely dry, then rub in a very thin final coat of oil [1]. Heating isn't about seasoning; it's about getting the wok properly dry, since a towel alone leaves some moisture behind [1].

**Cleaning:** For stuck-on food, heating the wok and then hitting it with water and scrubbing is a great way, and it won't damage the wok [2]. A bamboo wok brush is the best tool for that, though any scrubber works [2]. If the surface feels rough or catches a cloth, scrub it out [3]. I wouldn't use Bar Keepers Friend on a wok, because it's harsh and would likely remove the black oxide layer; a scrubby brush or bamboo brush, plus soap if needed, does the job [4].

**The oil coat:** Yes, heat to dry, then oil, but keep the oil to a minimum. The oil matters mostly if you're storing the wok where moisture in the air could reach it, because bare carbon steel can rust [5]. It matters less if you're cooking in it every day [5]. Wipe the oil out as if you'd put it in by accident, since a thick layer can turn gummy over time [6].

**If you have the nitrided wok:** The coat is less necessary, since it isn't reactive the way raw carbon steel is [5]. You also don't need to be as careful about drying it as you would with cast iron, but heat-drying still helps maintain the seasoning [7].

questions.question: A genuine question: if a wok doesn't build up layers of polymers like a cast iron, what does it mean for a wok to build up seasoning?

hybrid.answer:
For a wok, seasoning mostly means getting the raw carbon steel to turn into black oxide, not building up layers of polymer [1]. You heat the wok until the whole surface turns black or a bluish black [2]. After that, it's not something you build up over time. It's more of a per-use thing [3][4].

**Why polymer layers don't last in a wok:** the bottom gets very hot while the sides stay cooler. The metal expands unevenly, so hard polymer layers have a tough time sticking [5]. Sauces, often acidic, also strip the seasoning every time you cook [5].

**What I expect instead:** I don't expect or aim for a thick layer of seasoning in a wok [6]. Some carbonized, polymerized oil does get into your food as you cook, and that's part of the flavor of wok cooking [7]. At home I rub a very small amount of oil, about a quarter to half a teaspoon, into the wok with a paper towel before cooking [8].

questions.question: Is there any advantage to salting hours ahead of time with this technique, or does the long time the steak spends hanging out in the oven make that moot? [reverse sear]

hybrid.answer:
I haven't covered reverse searing or oven time in my videos, so I can't say whether the oven makes salting ahead moot. What I did test was a pan-seared tenderloin salted and left uncovered in the fridge overnight, compared with one salted just before cooking, and the advantages there were real.

- **Juiciness and tenderness:** Salt breaks down some of the muscle proteins and gets absorbed into the steak. That seasons it throughout and helps it hold moisture better and come out more tender [1].
- **Browning:** Leaving it uncovered dries the surface, which makes the steak easier to sear and gives a better browned crust [2]. The unsalted steak sizzled much harder in the pan, which is moisture evaporating off the surface, and evaporating water takes a lot of energy [3][4].
- **Result:** The salted steak had a nicer brown crust and a smooth juiciness, while the juices in the unsalted steak ran out quickly [5].

How much of this carries over to a slow oven stage, I haven't tested.

questions.question: So, Kenji, since you left Cook's Illustrated, they've started to advocate cold searing (starting in a cold pan and flipping every 2 minutes until done). What are your thoughts?

hybrid.answer: I haven't covered cold searing, or Cook's Illustrated's flip-every-two-minutes approach, in my videos yet, so I can't give you a verdict on it. The closest thing I've said is about my own method: the reverse sear is still my favorite way to cook a big steak [1]. It starts the steak in a low oven and finishes with a sear, which gives a much more even cook from edge to center, rather than the bullseye you get from the traditional sear-first method [2].
